answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1881–1973 · Spanish painter, sculptor & co-founder of Cubism
answer.sourceLine: This one is real, and unusually well documented. The sentence appears in “Picasso Speaks: A Statement by the Artist,” printed in the New York monthly The Arts, vol. 3, no. 5 (May 1923), p. 315 — Picasso’s statement to the critic Marius de Zayas. He spoke in Spanish and authenticated the Spanish text, but the magazine printed only the English rendering, which is the wording the world quotes.

source.heading: Where it actually appears

docMeta.dd: “Picasso Speaks: A Statement by the Artist”
The Arts (New York), vol. 3, no. 5, May 1923 — the quoted sentence on p. 315
Marius de Zayas, critic and caricaturist
Spoken in Spanish. Picasso authenticated the Spanish text, but the magazine printed only its English rendering — the wording quoted here.

source.excerpt: We all know that art is not truth. Art is a lie that makes us realize truth, at least the truth that is given us to understand. The artist must know the manner whereby to convince others of the truthfulness of his lies. If he only shows in his work that he has searched, and re-searched, for the way to put over his lies, he would never accomplish any thing.
trail: May 1923 — the New York monthly The Arts prints “Picasso Speaks: A Statement by the Artist.” Quote Investigator places the sentence ↗ in volume 3, number 5, on page 315 — the earliest attestation it documents.

The full statement survives in teaching editions. Columbia University’s Art Humanities reader reprints the complete English text ↗, citing “Picasso Speaks,” The Arts, New York, May 1923 — so the famous line can be read in the argument it belongs to.
1946 — QI notes the reprint ↗ of the 1923 statement in Alfred H. Barr Jr.’s Picasso: Fifty Years of His Art; that Museum of Modern Art volume is borrowable at the Internet Archive ↗.
30 July 1957 — a Leonard Lyons column in the Chicago Daily Defender renders it “Art is a lie that makes us see the truth,” one of the shortened forms QI traces ↗ through the following decades.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed as Quote Investigator prints the 1923 passage ↗. Reprints tidy the surrounding sentences a little — Columbia’s text ↗ reads “must know how to convince others” — but the famous sentence itself is identical in every version checked.

source.rightsNote: The statement was first published in The Arts (New York) in May 1923 — a United States publication well before the 1931 line, so both the piece and the English translation printed in it are in the public domain in the US. Note that this covers the 1923 magazine text only: later reprints carry their own editorial matter, and Alfred H. Barr Jr.’s 1946 Picasso: Fifty Years of His Art is a separate, later publication.

author.name: Pablo Picasso
author.heading: Who was Pablo Picasso?
author.metaLine: 1881–1973 · Spanish painter & sculptor · co-founder of Cubism
author.bio: Born in Málaga in 1881 and dead in 1973 at ninety-one, Pablo Picasso co-founded Cubism, invented constructed sculpture, and co-invented collage — then spent decades refusing to stay inside any one of those styles. He gave comparatively few formal statements about his own work, which is exactly why the 1923 piece in The Arts gets quoted so heavily: it is one of the rare occasions he sat down and explained himself at length. In it he is not being cryptic about art and truth — he is defending Cubism against critics who called it an experiment, and arguing that every school of painting, from the primitives to Ingres, traffics in convincing lies.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound — this really is Picasso. What gets mangled is the wording, and a family of shorter, punchier descendants that have drifted onto other names. If you have seen this quote on a poster, you have probably seen a paraphrase.

items.who: “Art is a lie that makes us see the truth”
items.why: The most common substitute. Quote Investigator dates this form ↗ to a Leonard Lyons “Lyons Den” column of 30 July 1957 in the Chicago Daily Defender, which used it while announcing Harold Clurman’s collection The Lie That Tells the Truth. Picasso’s 1923 text says realize, not see.

items.who: “Art is a lie that tells the truth”
items.why: The shortest and most quoted form, and the furthest from the page. It drops the qualifier that makes the sentence interesting — “at least the truth that is given us to understand.” QI tracks the “tells the truth” phrasing ↗ through a long line of later uses applied to fables, drama, literature and camp.

Cocteau wrote a genuinely separate, similar-sounding line — “je suis un mensonge qui dit toujours la vérité” (“I am a lie that always tells the truth”) — published in 1927, per Quote Investigator ↗. It is Cocteau’s, it postdates Picasso’s 1923 statement, and it is not this quote.
The variant “Fiction is the lie through which we tell the truth” was credited to Camus in 1995. QI judges that credit ↗ “too late to provide substantive evidence.”

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence on this page is Picasso’s own, printed in The Arts in May 1923 and reproduced in full by Columbia’s primary-source reader ↗. If your version says see or tells, you have a descendant, not the original.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Picasso was not delivering an aphorism about the nature of beauty. He was annoyed. The 1923 statement opens with him complaining that critics kept praising him for the “spirit of research,” as though Cubism were an experiment still working toward a result. “To search means nothing in painting,” he says. “To find is the thing.”

The line about lies is the pivot of that argument. If art were truth, then painting would be judged by how closely it matched the world — and Cubism would lose. Picasso’s move is to deny the premise for everyone at once: Velázquez’s Philip IV was surely not the man himself, yet nobody can now picture Philip IV any other way. From the primitives down to Ingres, he argues, there are only “forms which are more or less convincing lies.” Cubism is not a departure from painting’s job. It is painting’s job, admitted out loud.
context.detailsSummary: How the interview came to be printed in English
detailsBody: Marius de Zayas was a Mexican-born caricaturist and critic active in the New York avant-garde. Picasso gave him the statement in Spanish and then authenticated the Spanish text — but The Arts printed only the English translation, as Quote Investigator records ↗. That is why the famous sentence has no single “original” Spanish text in general circulation: the words everyone quotes are the 1923 magazine’s English rendering of a Spanish original the magazine chose not to print.

One practical consequence: later reprints are not always byte-identical. Quote Investigator and Wikiquote both give the 1923 clause as “The artist must know the manner whereby to convince others of the truthfulness of his lies,” while Columbia’s teaching reprint ↗ smooths it to “must know how to convince others.” The sentence quotle.info is checking — “Art is a lie that makes us realize truth, at least the truth that is given us to understand” — is identical in every version fetched.
context.pull: Nature and art, being two different things, cannot be the same thing.
